chapters.title: Let a Hot Feeling Cool Before You Act
chapters.hook: You are typing a furious reply, and every sharp word feels true. That certainty is the warning sign.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a strong feeling tells them what to do, and acting fast shows they mean it. Actually, the first urge is rarely your best thinking, because anger or fear takes over the mind and passes itself off as good sense.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a strong feeling hits, wait before you act, because the first urge is rarely your best thinking.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take the message or choice that has you most upset right now, and wait until tomorrow before you answer or decide.

memorableLines.text: The surer a hot feeling makes you, the longer your answer should wait.

breakdown.fastRead:
It is nine at night, and Noor is at the counter of her bike repair shop. A one-star review says she overcharged a customer and left his brakes worse. Her face burns. She types a reply calling him a liar, and she has never felt more right. Every future customer will see it.

Robert Greene, who writes about human nature, says no one is as rational as they think, including you. When anger or fear flares up, it takes over your thinking and feels like good sense. Pericles, who led ancient Athens, thought each problem through before he spoke. Under him the city kept steady through a long war with its rival Sparta. Then he died in a plague, and leaders ruled by passion took over. In a rush of hope and pride, Athens voted to invade Sicily. It ended in disaster.

The fix is time, and counting to three is not enough. Let the heat drop for an hour or a night, then decide. You are not burying the feeling, only taking back the wheel. Noor saves the reply as a draft. In the morning she checks the work order and writes a short, polite answer offering to recheck the brakes. Wait before you act when a strong feeling grabs you, and your clearer thinking gets the final say.

breakdown.fullRead:
It is nine at night, and Noor is at the counter of her bike repair shop. A one-star review says she overcharged a customer and left his brakes worse. She remembers the job, and she is sure the brakes were fine. Her face burns. She types a reply calling him a liar, and she has never felt more right. Every future customer will see it.

If she posts it, readers will not judge the brakes. They will judge an owner who fights with customers online. Yet posting feels like standing up for herself. Most people trust a strong feeling this way. It seems to be telling you what to do, and acting fast seems to prove you mean it. That rush of being sure is exactly the moment to stop.

Robert Greene, a writer on power and human behavior, calls this the law of irrationality. No one is as rational as they think, including you. Feelings bend your thinking all day long, and the first step is to admit it. Much of the bending is quiet and steady. You notice only the facts that prove you right. You blame other people when things go wrong. Greene calls this low-grade irrationality, and it tilts nearly every judgment you make.

The second kind is louder. Greene calls it high-grade irrationality, the flare-up when anger, fear or greed takes over completely. He calls the things that set it off inflaming factors, and he names five. There are old wounds from early life that a word or a tone can reopen. There are sudden gains or losses, and pressure that keeps building. There are certain people who know how to stir you up, and there is the pull of a crowd. In a flare-up the feeling passes itself off as good sense. You still think, but your thinking now works for the feeling.

His proof is Pericles, who led ancient Athens. Pericles had a habit of stepping back from the heat of the moment. He thought a problem through before he spoke, and he stayed calm when others were stirred up. Under him the city kept a careful course, even through a long war with its rival Sparta.

Then plague struck Athens, and Pericles died of it. The leaders who took his place were ruled by passion, and the city lurched from one bold venture to the next. The worst was a voyage to conquer Sicily. Excited Athenians voted for it in a rush of hope and pride. Nobody paused long enough to think it through, and it ended in disaster. The city had the same people as before. What it had lost was a leader who made it wait.

Greene's method has three steps. First, see your own steady biases. Second, watch for the things that set off your flare-ups. Third, bring out what he calls your rational self, the calmer side that sees what is really going on. You do this by knowing yourself well and tracing each feeling back to where it started. You accept people as they are instead of wishing they were different. You look for the balance where thought and feeling work together, and you learn to enjoy clear thinking for its own sake. Above all, you give yourself more time before you react. Counting to three is not enough. Let the heat drop for an hour or a night, then decide.

The aim is not to kill the feeling. It is to see it clearly, so it stops steering you without your knowing. You are not burying it, only taking back the wheel. Noor saves the reply as a draft. In the morning she checks the work order. The brakes were fine, but the anger has drained away, and she can see what a public fight would cost. She writes a short, polite answer with the facts and offers to recheck the brakes for free. Wait before you act when a strong feeling grabs you, and your clearer thinking gets the final say.

examples.title: The deal a teammate closed
examples.scenario: Kwame has chased a chain of dental clinics for six weeks. At the four o'clock sales huddle, his manager announces that Rhea closed the deal after one phone call. Rhea smiles at him across the table. Kwame's neck goes hot. He is sure she used his notes from the shared folder, and his hand is already half raised to say so.
examples.whatToDo: Lower the hand and let the huddle end. Tonight, check the folder's history, then decide whether to raise it with Rhea.
examples.whyItMatters: An accusation made in front of the whole team can't be taken back, even if the folder later shows he was wrong.

examples.title: Counting to ten in the cafeteria
examples.scenario: Last month a classmate mocked Ines's science presentation. She counted to ten, then said something cruel back and landed in detention. Today in the cafeteria the same boy laughs at her sneakers loud enough for the whole table to hear. She starts counting again, but by eight her fists are tight and the comeback is ready.
examples.whatToDo: Pick up her tray, move to another table, and wait until after school to decide if the comment deserves any answer.
examples.whyItMatters: Ten seconds left her anger at full heat. A few hours let it drop, so she can choose with a clear head.

examples.title: A scraped car at eleven at night
examples.scenario: At eleven at night, Olumide's sixteen-year-old son calls. He scraped the family car along a parking post, and he is not hurt. Olumide's fear turns to fury within a minute. He plans to take the keys for a year and announce it the moment his son walks in. The front door opens, and the boy says, "Dad, I'm so sorry."
examples.whatToDo: Hug his son, say they will talk about the car tomorrow, and set the punishment once the fear has passed.
examples.whyItMatters: Decided in the morning, the punishment fits what happened, not how scared Olumide felt at eleven at night.

questions.prompt: At the end-of-season party for the kids' soccer team you coach, another parent says the team lost because of your coaching. Your heart is pounding. What do you do?
choices: Say you'll think about it, and reply once you're home and calm.
Answer firmly right there, so the other parents see you won't be pushed.
Ask the club's coordinator to step in and settle the complaint.
questions.explanation: At home, with your heart slowed, you can decide what the remark deserves. Answering firmly on the spot feels strong, but that is the pounding heart choosing your words in front of everyone.

questions.prompt: A café owner is furious when her milk supplier gets the order wrong for the third time. That night she writes an email ending their deal. She waits until morning, then sends it unchanged. Weeks later she regrets it. What belief tripped her up?
choices: Thinking one night was enough, when she needed a full week.
Thinking email was the right way to end it.
Thinking the wait counted, when she'd decided while still angry.
questions.explanation: Waiting only helps if you decide after the heat drops. She made the choice in anger and just sent it later. A longer wait with the same email would have changed nothing.

questions.prompt: In the middle of a busy dinner service, a chef gets a harsh note from the owner about his new dish. He wants to walk out on the spot. Instead he finishes the shift and sleeps on it before doing anything. What most likely happens next?
choices: His anger fades by then, so he lets the note slide.
He talks through the dish with a clear head and keeps his job.
The owner reads the late reply as weakness and treats him with less respect.
questions.explanation: By the next day the heat has dropped, so he can speak about the dish instead of quitting in a rage. Waiting is not burying the feeling. He still raises it, just calmly.

questions.prompt: An hour ago your friend's manager turned down her request for a raise. She texts you: "I'm writing my resignation letter now, while I still have the nerve." What is your best reply?
choices: "Go ask your manager right now exactly why it was turned down."
"Save the letter and read it again tomorrow before you decide."
"Walk around the block first, then hand it in."
questions.explanation: An hour is too soon, and the sting of the no is still deciding for her. Reading it tomorrow lets the heat drop. A walk around the block is only a short pause, and the anger is still there after.

questions.prompt: A teacher gets an angry email from a parent at lunch. She leaves it alone until evening, then sends a short, kind and clear reply. The parent thanks her. Why did the wait help?
choices: By evening her anger had faded, so a cool head picked the words.
By evening the parent had cooled off, so the reply landed softly.
A slower reply showed the worried parent that she was taking the email seriously.
questions.explanation: At lunch the anger would have chosen her words. Waiting let it fade so she could answer calmly. The parent may also have cooled, but the change that shaped the reply was in her.

questions.prompt: Three days ago your roommate ate the cake you'd bought for your partner's birthday. You said nothing while you cooled off, and today you feel calm. What is your move now?
choices: Let it go, since the anger is gone and the birthday is long over.
Bring it up as a joke at dinner, to keep things light.
Tell your roommate calmly why it bothered you, and agree on a fix.
questions.explanation: The wait was for the heat to drop, not for the problem to vanish. Now you can raise it with a clear head. Letting it go just buries the feeling instead of dealing with it.

questions.prompt: Down one goal near the end, a team captain sees the referee make a bad call. She sprints over and argues on the spot to show she won't let it pass. She gets a yellow card, and her team loses focus. Where did her thinking go wrong?
choices: Thinking that arguing at once showed how much the call mattered.
Thinking a referee will change a call if a captain pushes hard enough.
Thinking one bad call was worth a fight on the field.
questions.explanation: Arguing on the spot felt like proof she cared, but it was the anger acting. She could have raised the call calmly at the break. The call itself may well have been worth questioning.

reviewCards.front: Your landlord texts that the rent is going up next month, and you want to call right now and say you're moving out.
reviewCards.back: Put the phone down and let the shock settle overnight. Decide about moving once the heat has dropped, when you can weigh it clearly.

reviewCards.front: Why is the urge you feel in the first minutes of anger a poor guide to what you should do?
reviewCards.back: Because a strong feeling takes over your thinking and feels like good sense, so the move it pushes is rarely your clearest one.

reviewCards.front: Once the heat of a strong feeling has dropped, the next step is ...
reviewCards.back: ... to decide and act with a clear head, not to bury the feeling and stay quiet.

reviewCards.front: A man felt so hurt by a friend's joke at a wedding that he left early and ignored her calls for a month.
reviewCards.back: He acted while the hurt was at its hottest. A night's wait would have let him decide calmly whether to talk to her about the joke.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should you do when a strong feeling hits, and why?
reviewCards.back: Hold off on acting until the heat drops, because the first urge feels right but is rarely your best thinking.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Putting real time between a hot feeling and what you do about it, so a calm mind makes the call.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to answer my messages after lunch, I save any reply I write while annoyed as a draft and reread it an hour later.
When I notice I'm halfway through a sharp reply or a snap decision, I stop, step away from the screen or the room, and decide only once the heat has dropped.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, think of one choice you made in anger or fear this month. Write down what you did, then what you would choose now with a clear head.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each week, list the moments a strong feeling pushed you to act fast. Mark the ones you waited on, and compare how those turned out with the rest.

chapters.title: Your First Read of People Is Only a Guess
chapters.hook: You can tell what a stranger is like before your coffee cools. That feeling of knowing is mostly your own mood looking back at you.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels natural to trust your quick read of a person, since you are good with people. But a first read is a guess to test, because your own needs and moods fill in whatever you have not yet seen.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before you judge someone, assume you don't understand them yet, then read their mood and test your guess.
chapters.tryThisNow: In your next conversation today, notice the other person's mood, make a guess about why, then ask one question that tests it.

memorableLines.text: Treat every first impression as a draft, then let the person edit it.

breakdown.fastRead:
A new teammate sits through her first lunch with your group, eyes on her phone. Is she shy, stuck-up, or bored with you? How would you know, when your own worries answer first? Guess wrong, and you may freeze out a future friend.

Robert Greene says everyone is wrapped up in themselves, you included. That self-love, which he calls narcissism, turns harmful only when it stays pointed inward. Then your own worries fill in what you can't see. First, assume you don't understand the person yet. Read their mood in their face and voice. Test your guess against what they do, and correct it. The explorer Ernest Shackleton saw the Antarctic ice crush his ship, Endurance, stranding his crew far from home. He read each man's mood and stepped in before gloom could spread. Every man came home alive.

Feeling good with people is the trap, since once you're sure, you stop looking. So you watch. She looks up whenever the table laughs, nervous rather than bored. You test it by asking about her last job, and she lights up. Once you doubt your first read, watch the mood and test your guess, you see the person instead of your own fears.

breakdown.fullRead:
A new teammate sits through her first lunch with your group, eyes on her phone. Is she shy, stuck-up, or bored with you? How would you know, when your own worries answer first? Your gut has a verdict before the sandwiches are gone. Guess wrong, and you may freeze out a future friend, or warm to someone who will cost you later. Most people seldom find out how often they guess wrong, because they don't check.

Robert Greene says everyone is wrapped up in themselves, you included. All day you carry thoughts about how you look, what you need and who has slighted you. That self-love, which he calls narcissism, is not the problem. It turns harmful only when it stays pointed inward. Then you live inside your own head, and your needs fill in whatever you can't see about other people. A quiet colleague becomes cold. A busy friend becomes careless. You are reading yourself and calling it them.

Greene places everyone somewhere on a line. At one end is the deep narcissist, a person with no solid sense of who they are. With nothing steady inside, they feed on other people's attention. At the other end is the healthy narcissist. Their sense of self is solid enough that their attention can flow outward, toward other people. The goal is to move toward that end and turn your self-love into empathy, the ability to feel and understand what someone else feels.

Empathy, he argues, is a skill, and it comes in steps. The first is an attitude. You assume you don't understand the person yet, however sure your gut feels. That small doubt keeps you looking. The second step he calls visceral empathy, which means catching someone's mood the way you feel a change in the weather. You watch the face, the voice, the way they sit or stand. Shoulders that tighten when a topic comes up can tell you more than anything said aloud.

The third step he calls analytic empathy. You learn the person's history and what they value, so you can see why they feel what they feel. The last step is the skill itself. You check your reading against what the person actually does, and you correct it when you were wrong. Each correction sharpens the next read.

His clearest example is Ernest Shackleton, an explorer whose ship, Endurance, was crushed by the Antarctic ice. The crew was stranded far from home. Cold and hunger were one danger. Despair was another, because one man's gloom could spread through the whole camp. Shackleton read each man closely. He noticed who was going quiet, who was growing short-tempered and who was losing hope, and he stepped in before the mood could spread. He held the crew together, and every one of them came home alive.

The usual answer is to trust your gut, because you're good with people. That feeling is the trap. The moment you feel sure, you stop looking, and the gaps fill with your own worries. Shackleton could not afford that kind of certainty about his men. A snap judgment about a teammate costs less than a frozen camp, but it goes wrong the same way.

So you watch her through the rest of lunch. She looks up whenever the table laughs, then down again, nervous rather than bored. You test it by asking about her last job, and she lights up. Had she shrugged, you would have changed your guess and kept watching. Once you doubt your first read, watch the mood and test your guess, you see the person instead of your own fears.

examples.title: Third cancelled game night
examples.scenario: Idris's friend Dario has cancelled their Friday board-game night for the third time, with a short text: "Can't tonight, sorry." After ten years of friendship, Idris reads it as Dario drifting away. He has already typed back "No worries, I'll stop asking," and it feels fair. His thumb hovers over send.
examples.whatToDo: Delete the reply. Assume you don't know why yet, call Dario instead, listen to how he sounds, and ask what's going on.
examples.whyItMatters: A tired voice tells Idris more than a short text, and one question checks his guess before he ends a long friendship.

examples.title: The barista who went quiet
examples.scenario: Rosa runs a small bakery cafe and prides herself on reading people. Her new barista, Teo, rarely smiles at customers, so on his second day she decided he had a poor attitude. She took him aside by the espresso machine for a friendly talk about warmth. Since then he speaks even less, and this morning he asked to drop his Saturday shifts.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the label. Watch Teo through one busy hour, notice when his face tightens, then ask him about that exact moment.
examples.whyItMatters: Her quick read already cost her a good worker's trust. A guess she checks can still win it back.

examples.title: Told to rinse her fast and move on
examples.scenario: Anouk is an apprentice at a hair salon. A client, Mrs. Varga, snaps at her about the water temperature, and the senior stylist, Bram, rolls his eyes. "She's like that every visit," he says. "Rinse her fast and move on." But Anouk saw the client touch a thin patch near her crown twice, then go stiff at the mirror. She feels torn, since Bram has worked here for years.
examples.whatToDo: Don't argue with Bram. Hold both reads as guesses, and test yours by quietly offering to give her crown more volume.
examples.whyItMatters: If Mrs. Varga softens, Anouk has seen what Bram missed for years. If she doesn't, Anouk corrects her guess and keeps watching.

questions.prompt: Your new neighbor never waves back when you wave from the driveway each morning. After two weeks you decide he's unfriendly and stop waving. Where did you slip up?
choices: Taking his silence to heart instead of simply letting it go.
Calling him unfriendly without once checking that guess with him.
Not asking the other neighbors about him before deciding.
questions.explanation: Two weeks of no waves gave you a guess, not an answer. One short hello would have tested it, since he may be shy or not see you. Other neighbors would only hand you their own guesses.

questions.prompt: On a group hike, your usually chatty friend goes quiet and drops to the back. You start to think she's annoyed with you. Instead you walk beside her, see her wince on each downhill step, and ask about her boots. What most likely happens?
choices: You find out it's her sore heel, not you, and slow the pace.
You confirm your first hunch that she is quietly upset with you.
She shrugs it off, so you go back to guessing she's annoyed with you.
questions.explanation: Walking beside her let you read what her body showed, and asking about the boots tested that guess. Your first hunch came from your own worry, so it had little to do with her.

questions.prompt: A friend on your Sunday soccer team says, "I can size anyone up in five minutes. The new striker is arrogant." What would be the most useful thing to say back?
choices: "You're probably right. Your first read of people is usually sound."
"Be extra friendly to him, and he'll stop acting so cocky around you."
"Maybe. Watch him after a bad pass and see if it holds."
questions.explanation: Watching him after a bad pass shows his real mood, and seeing whether the read holds tests it. Being extra friendly treats arrogance as a fact and tries to fix something nobody has checked.

questions.prompt: A team lead decided his quiet coworker didn't care about their weekly meetings. Then he noticed she leaned forward whenever costs came up. He asked what she'd cut from the budget, and her answer saved the team a month. Why did it pay off?
choices: He treated his first idea of her as a guess and checked it.
Putting her on the spot pushed her to finally speak up.
Asking any quiet coworker for their ideas will get them talking sooner or later.
questions.explanation: Her leaning forward didn't fit his first label, and asking about costs tested the new read. A general call for ideas could easily have missed the one topic she cared about.

questions.prompt: You arrive at a family dinner, and your brother gives you a flat hello and turns away. Your gut says he's still angry about last month's argument. What's your move?
choices: Bring up last month's argument right away and clear the air.
Watch how he is with everyone tonight before deciding it's about you.
Send him a careful message later that night explaining your side of it.
questions.explanation: Watching him with everyone tests whether the flat hello is about you at all. Raising the argument right away acts on a guess you haven't checked, and could start a fight over nothing.

questions.prompt: A coach in an adult basketball league benches a player, who then sits sulking at the end of the bench. She guesses he resents her and asks him. He says he's worn out from his night job. She nods, but keeps treating him like a sulker. Where is the trap?
choices: Asking him straight out when she could have just watched longer.
Benching him in the first place while he was so worn out from work.
Hearing that her guess was off and not changing her view of him.
questions.explanation: Asking was a fair test, and it showed her guess was wrong. Testing only helps if she corrects the read, yet she kept the old one. Watching longer changes nothing if she ignores what she learns.

questions.prompt: A new tenant prides herself on reading people fast. Her landlord answers her first call with a few curt words, and she decides he's hunting for a reason to keep her deposit. How is this likely to play out?
choices: Standing firm early makes the landlord back off and treat her more fairly.
Each short reply looks like more proof, and things between them sour.
His curtness fades by itself once he gets to know her.
questions.explanation: Once she's sure, she stops looking and her worry fills every gap, so each curt reply reads as an attack. She never checks whether he's just busy. Standing firm answers a threat she hasn't confirmed.

reviewCards.front: Why does your quick read of a new person so often miss?
reviewCards.back: Because your own needs and worries fill in everything you haven't seen yet, so you end up reading yourself instead of them.

reviewCards.front: Before deciding what someone is like, first assume ...
reviewCards.back: ... you don't understand them yet. Then watch their mood, and check your guess against what they actually do.

reviewCards.front: A man decided his new flatmate was rude because she never joined shared dinners, so he stopped inviting her. Months later he learned she worked evenings. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He turned a first read into a verdict and never tested it. One question about her schedule would have corrected the guess months earlier.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what three moves help you read a person well?
reviewCards.back: Assume, read, test: admit you don't know them yet, notice their mood, then check your guess and fix it when it's wrong.

reviewCards.front: Your sister picks up your call with a flat "What?" and a sharp reply is already forming in your head.
reviewCards.back: Hold it. Ask how her day is going, listen to her voice, and see whether the flatness has anything to do with you.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Seeing people as they really are, not as your own worries paint them.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself deciding what someone is like after one exchange, I call it a guess and look for one sign that could prove it wrong.
When I sit down across from someone for a meeting or a meal, I spend the first minute watching their face and voice before I talk about myself.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one person you've already made up your mind about, like a quiet coworker or a curt neighbor. Before the day is out, ask them one easy question that could prove your view wrong, and watch how they answer.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, think back to one person whose mood you guessed at, maybe at work or at a family meal. Compare your guess with what they did next, and change your view of them if it didn't hold.

chapters.title: Believe the Face When the Words Say Otherwise
chapters.hook: You tell yourself that careful listening shows what people feel. Then a friend says she's fine through a clenched jaw, and you believe her.
chapters.counterintuition: You have probably been told that to understand someone, you should hang on their every word. The trouble is that words are the part people control best, so watch the face and voice, where real feelings slip out.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When someone's words and body disagree, believe the body, because feelings leak out through face and voice.
chapters.tryThisNow: Ask one person you see today how their week is really going, and watch their face and voice as they answer.

memorableLines.text: Words are what people choose to show; the face shows what they feel.

breakdown.fastRead:
The words people say are often the least honest thing about them. Milton Erickson learned this as a teenager, when polio left him paralyzed in bed, able only to watch his family. Their faces and tones kept saying something different from their words. Someone could say no in a way that meant yes. He later built a career as a psychiatrist, a doctor of the mind, on that skill.

We miss the rest because we are wrapped up in ourselves and in the words. Robert Greene says everyone wears a mask, a polite face put on for others. Words are the easiest part of it to control. Feelings leak out through a tight smile or a flat voice, and almost nobody watches closely. Greene would have you stop leaning on words, and watch for the places where words and body clash.

Say you ask your coworker Kofi to cover your Friday shift. He says sure, but his eyes drop and his voice goes flat. Believe the voice. Don't call it out, or the mask goes back up. Ask something that makes honesty easy, like what would make Friday work for him. He admits his son has a match, and you avoid a quiet grudge. Stop taking people at their word when their face says otherwise, and believe what their body lets slip instead.
breakdown.deepRead:
The words people say are often the least honest thing about them. Their face and voice usually tell you more. Milton Erickson learned this as a teenager, when polio left him paralyzed and stuck in bed. He could not join in, so he watched and listened to his family. Slowly he saw that their faces and tones often said something different from their words. A person could say no in a way that clearly meant yes. The mouth said the polite thing, and the body gave away the real feeling. He later built a whole career as a psychiatrist, a doctor of the mind, on that skill.

Most of us were raised to listen to words. In most talks we are also busy with ourselves, planning what to say next. Robert Greene argues that this leaves us easy to fool. People wear masks, polite faces put on to fit in, and words are the part of the mask they control best.

The face, the voice and the body are much harder to steer. Feelings leak through them all day long. Watch for a smile that stops short of the eyes, a voice gone flat, a body leaning away. Almost nobody pays close attention, Greene says, so the few who do have a real edge. So he would have you stop leaning on words, and watch for the places where words and body clash.

Say you ask your coworker Kofi to cover your Friday shift. He says sure, no problem, but his eyes drop and his voice goes flat. First, notice that the words and the body disagree. Then believe the body, which is saying no, or at least maybe. Don't call out the slip, since naming it only pushes the mask back up. Instead, ask something that makes honesty easy, like what would make Friday work for him. He admits his son has a match that evening. You find someone else, and Kofi doesn't spend the next month quietly resenting you. Stop taking people at their word when their face says otherwise, and believe what their body lets slip instead.

examples.title: A smile at the repair counter
examples.scenario: Rafael has just finished a brake job at his small garage, and the customer is at the counter paying. She says, "Great, thanks, all good," but she keeps tapping the labor line on the invoice, and her smile drops the moment she looks down. Her card is already in the reader. He can hand back the keys or say something first.
examples.whatToDo: Believe the tapping finger over the "all good." Ask her, "Did anything on the bill surprise you?" and walk her through the labor line.
examples.whyItMatters: A customer who pays with a smile but leaves annoyed rarely comes back. Clearing it up at the counter keeps her business.

examples.title: The garden schedule everyone said was fine
examples.scenario: Manon runs the community garden on her street. At the last meeting she proposed a new watering schedule, went round the circle, and listened hard to every answer, writing each one down. Everyone said it was fine. Three weeks later, half the tomato beds are dry, two longtime members have stopped coming, and nobody will say why.
examples.whatToDo: At the next meeting, watch faces as the schedule comes up. Later, quietly ask anyone who went still or looked away which hours would really suit them.
examples.whyItMatters: Her notebook held only the polite answers. The real ones were on the faces in that circle, and they decide who keeps showing up.

examples.title: Driving lessons with a hovering foot
examples.scenario: Tomasz has his driving test in two weeks. On roundabouts, his instructor Gloria says, "Good, fine," but her foot hovers over her own brake pedal and her voice turns clipped. Last lesson he noticed and asked, "Was that okay?" She said, "Yes, fine," and moved on. Now he dreads the test and still has no idea what he's doing wrong.
examples.whatToDo: Keep trusting her foot, but swap the yes-or-no question for an open one, like "What's the one thing you'd fix on that roundabout?"
examples.whyItMatters: A yes-or-no question invites the same polite yes. An open one makes the honest answer the easy one to give.

questions.prompt: A dog walker tells a client his price is going up next month. She says, "That's fine," but her voice goes flat and she looks away. He asks what would make the new price work for her. What most likely happens next?
choices: She repeats that it's fine, and the flat tone meant nothing.
She feels watched and caught out, and she quietly starts looking for another walker.
She admits the price stretches her budget, and they agree on fewer walks.
questions.explanation: Her flat voice and the look away showed the price bothered her, and his open question made the honest answer easy. She's unlikely to feel caught out, because he asked about her needs instead of naming the slip.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My new roommate told me she doesn't mind my drumming at night. She had a tight smile and kept rubbing her temples, but she said yes. So I'm fine, right?" What's your best reply?
choices: She said yes out loud, so take her at her word.
Her face said no, so ask which hours would really suit her.
Tell her the tight smile gave her away, and ask why she lied.
questions.explanation: The tight smile and rubbed temples were her real answer, and asking about hours lets her say so. Telling her she lied would only push the polite mask back up.

questions.prompt: A nurse asks a patient how bad his pain is. He says, "Not too bad," but grips the bed rail and his voice shakes. She trusts the grip and calls the doctor. Why is the grip the better guide?
choices: He chose his words to sound brave, but the grip came out unplanned.
Patients often mix up their words when they feel tired or scared.
A tight grip measures pain more exactly than any words a patient could find.
questions.explanation: His words were picked to sound brave, while the grip and shaky voice slipped out without a plan. He didn't mix up his words. He said just what he meant to say, and his body told the truth.

questions.prompt: You pitch a new idea to your manager. She says, "Interesting, let me think about it," while leaning back with her arms crossed and her eyes on her phone. What is your next move?
choices: Ask her to approve the budget now, while the idea feels fresh.
Send her a fuller write-up tonight with all the details.
Read it as a polite no, and ask what worries her.
questions.explanation: Crossed arms and eyes on her phone say she isn't sold, whatever her polite words suggest. Asking what worries her brings out the real answer. Pushing for the budget now ignores the no her body already gave.

questions.prompt: A team lead runs weekly check-ins through a written form and reads every answer closely. Everyone writes that things are fine. Then two people quit in the same month. Where did the lead go wrong?
choices: Checking in once a week, which was far too seldom to catch problems early.
Letting people answer without promising them it would stay private.
Trusting written answers, with no face or voice to check them against.
questions.explanation: A form holds only the words people choose, and feelings leak out through face and voice. Checking in more often wouldn't help when every check is still a written fine.

questions.prompt: A tutor sees a student nod and say, "Yes, I get it," while frowning at the page. The tutor says, "Your face says you don't get it at all. Why pretend?" How is the student likely to respond?
choices: The student insists it makes sense and hides the frown from then on.
The student feels truly seen and explains exactly which step was confusing.
The student stops bothering to hide the frown, since the confusion is now out.
questions.explanation: Naming the slip out loud pushes the mask back up, so the student defends the yes and hides the frown. A gentle, open question would have made the honest answer easier than the polite one.

questions.prompt: A friend tells you, "My business partner agreed to my plan by text, with smiley faces. But on our call, his voice went flat when we talked about the plan. What should I make of that?" What do you say back?
choices: Get his agreement signed on paper now, so he can't back out later.
Take the flat voice as his answer, and ask what bothers him.
Let it go, since a flat voice may mean a long day.
questions.explanation: His voice went flat on the plan itself, so the doubt is about the plan. Asking what bothers him brings it out now. A signature just locks in a partner who isn't on board.

reviewCards.front: When a person's yes comes with a flat voice and eyes that slide away, the part to believe is ...
reviewCards.back: ... the flat voice and the eyes. The yes was picked to be polite, while the tone slipped out on its own.

reviewCards.front: A roofer asked a homeowner if his quote looked okay. She said, "Sure," with a long sigh and a glance at the floor. He booked the job, and she cancelled two days later. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He went by the word and missed the sigh and the glance, which showed her doubts. One open question about the price could have brought them out while there was still time.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, when what someone says and how they look don't match, which do you go by?
reviewCards.back: Go by the face, voice and posture. People pick their words to fit the moment, but the real feeling slips out through the body.

reviewCards.front: Your teenager says the new school is great, but answers in one word with shoulders slumped. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Take the slumped shoulders as the truer answer. Don't call it out; ask something open, like which part of the day drags, and watch the face as the answer comes.

reviewCards.front: Why do face and voice give away feelings that words hide?
reviewCards.back: People plan their words, but they can't fully steer their face and voice. So the real feeling leaks out, and most listeners never notice it.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Catching the moment a person's face or voice tells a different story than their words, and going by that story.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I notice someone's tone or face doesn't match what they're saying, I treat the tone or face as the real answer and ask one open question that makes honesty easy.
When I ask someone at home how their day went, I watch their face and listen to their tone before I answer, not just their words.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day is over, ask someone for a small favor in person. Watch whether their face and voice agree with their answer, and if they don't, ask one open question.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, after your regular meeting or family dinner, jot down one moment when someone's words and face didn't match, and what you did about it.

chapters.title: Judge People by Their Record, Not Their Pitch
chapters.hook: A builder sketches your new kitchen on a napkin, and you're sold in ten minutes. His last two kitchens sat half-built for months.
chapters.counterintuition: If someone is brilliant and convincing, they'll do great this time. It sounds right, and it fails for one reason: a great pitch shows what someone could do, while habits decide what they will do. Their record tells you what comes next.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Judge people by what they have done over and over, not by their charm, talent or promises.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one person whose promise you're counting on today, and list what they did the last three times before you rely on it.

memorableLines.text: A pitch shows who someone hopes to be. Their record shows who they are.

breakdown.fastRead:
Matteo has his pen over a contract for the kitchen he saved two years to redo. The builder sketched the room on a napkin, and Matteo is sold. Someone that sharp, he figures, must do great work. Yet talent, charm and what people say about themselves show what they can do, not what they keep doing.

Robert Greene says what people keep doing comes from their character, the deep patterns laid down early in life. People repeat them over and over, mostly without seeing them. Howard Hughes, an American who made films and built planes, had huge talent, a family fortune and a bold image. Studios, investors and the government kept handing him big projects. Time after time, he insisted on deciding every detail himself, and the projects stalled, ran over budget or fell apart. He repeated the pattern to the end and finished his days shut away from the world.

The record, not the pitch, is the best guide to what someone will do next. Matteo puts down the pen and calls two past clients. Both describe a fast start, then months of bare walls and unanswered calls. He hires a quieter builder with a clean record. What a person has done again and again predicts what they will do next far better than charm or promises.

Someone that sharp, he figures, must do great work. He has not asked a single past client how their job went, and his savings ride on a ten-minute show.

What they keep doing decides how the next job goes.

Robert Greene calls what people keep doing their character. The word comes from an old Greek word for a mark cut or stamped into something, and the picture fits. Character is the set of deep patterns laid down early in life, then cut deeper by habit. People repeat those patterns over and over, in new jobs, new homes and new friendships, mostly without seeing them. Past behavior is the best guide to what someone will do next. The same forces are at work in you.

Howard Hughes shows how well talent can hide a pattern. He was an American who made films and built planes, with huge talent, a family fortune and a bold public image. To the world he looked like a daring man who could do anything. Film studios, investors and the government kept trusting him with big projects and big sums of money.

In his films, his aircraft work and the businesses he ran, the same thing kept happening. He insisted on deciding every detail himself, even where others had been hired to decide. The projects stalled, ran over budget or fell apart. Each time, people dazzled by his gifts bet on him again, and each time they met the same pattern.

That need for control was set early in his life, and he never broke free of it. He repeated it to the end and finished his days shut away from the world. Those who kept backing him were looking at his gifts and his image. His record told a different story, and it had been telling it all along.

So set the pitch aside and look at the record. Ask the people who were there what this person did again and again. Greene points to three places where a pattern shows. Watch how someone acts under stress and how they handle power. Watch, too, what they do in small moments when they think no one is looking. He also names types to steer clear of. One is the big talker, who promises much and finishes little. Another is the extreme perfectionist, who must control every detail. Then turn the same eye on yourself, so you can build on your good patterns instead of being ruled by the rest.

Matteo puts down the pen and calls two past clients. Both describe a fast start, then months of bare walls and unanswered calls. The builder's charm was real, and so was his pattern. Matteo hires a quieter builder with a clean record, and his savings go into a kitchen that gets finished. What a person has done again and again predicts what they will do next far better than charm or promises.

examples.title: A brother-in-law's third big plan
examples.scenario: Hana's brother-in-law wants to borrow three thousand dollars to start a food truck. Over dinner he flips through a sharp plan on his tablet, with menus, prices and a logo. She is impressed. She also remembers the phone repair stand and the online shoe shop, both dropped within months, both loans still half unpaid. He looks up and waits for her answer.
examples.whatToDo: Let the two dropped businesses and unpaid loans count for more than tonight's slick plan, and kindly say no.
examples.whyItMatters: He has quit the same way twice, so a third business will most likely end the same way, taking her money with it.

examples.title: The schedule on the fridge
examples.scenario: For the last three book reports, Jun's son Theo swore he would start early, and each time Jun believed him. This time Theo even drew a color-coded schedule and taped it to the fridge, so Jun stepped back. On Sunday at ten at night, Theo was in tears over a blank poster board, and Jun was driving to an all-night store for glue.
examples.whatToDo: Plan for the pattern, not the chart: sit with Theo for twenty minutes every Tuesday and Thursday from the day a report is set.
examples.whyItMatters: Four late reports say more about the next one than any schedule, and early check-ins fit the way Theo really works.

examples.title: Two alarms on the night shift
examples.scenario: Adaeze is running the night shift at a care home. A resident falls in the hallway just as an oxygen alarm sounds two doors down. She has seconds to send someone to the fall. Sione, an aide, has calmly handled every fall on this floor for two years. A nurse on her first night here steps forward first: "I did six years in emergency. I've got this."
examples.whatToDo: Send Sione to the fall he has handled so many times, and take the new nurse with you to the oxygen alarm.
examples.whyItMatters: With only seconds, there is no time to test a claim, and Sione's two years with falls are the surest record on the floor.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My new business partner is brilliant, and investors love her pitch. Her last two companies closed within a year, but I'm sure this one will last." What's your best reply?
choices: Talk to her last two partners about how those companies ended, before you sign.
Get a lawyer to write a strong contract, so you're covered if things go badly.
Watch how she handles the next tough investor meeting, and then decide.
questions.explanation: Two companies closing fast may be her pattern, and the people who were there can say what she kept doing. One investor meeting is a single show, and a contract only softens a loss you already chose.

questions.prompt: A community theater needs a treasurer. One volunteer gives a dazzling talk about budgets. The group instead picks a quiet member who has kept the books for its bake sales for six years, with every cent in place. A year later the accounts are spotless. Why did the choice work?
choices: The group picked someone humble, and humble people make the best treasurers.
Six years of honest books showed how she handles money, and people keep their patterns.
A small theater can check every receipt itself, so almost any treasurer would have done fine.
questions.explanation: Six years of careful books was a pattern, and it held for the next year. Being quiet was not the point, since a quiet person with messy books would have been a poor pick.

questions.prompt: You run a small design studio. A freelance artist with a stunning portfolio has missed the deadline on all three jobs he did for you, each time with a warm, funny apology. Now a big client job comes in, with a hard date. What's your move?
choices: Give him the job, after you explain why this one deadline matters so much to the studio.
Give him the job, but have him promise in writing to finish on time.
Give the big job to someone who hits deadlines, and keep him on flexible work.
questions.explanation: Three missed deadlines are his pattern, and his talent has not changed it. A written promise is still only words, and the last three jobs show how his dates tend to go.

questions.prompt: A hiring manager reads a résumé from a candidate who says he led two big projects at famous companies. In the interview he is funny and sharp. Because his résumé looks so strong, she skips calling his past bosses. Where is the trap here?
choices: Treating his own résumé as his record, instead of hearing how he acted on those projects.
Trusting a candidate who is funny, when humor in interviews often covers weak skills.
Making the offer before giving him a real skills test to prove he can do the work.
questions.explanation: A résumé is what he says about himself. His past bosses could say what he did again and again. A skills test would only show talent, and talent was never the doubt.

questions.prompt: A band's new guitarist has quit his last three bands, each time after a fight over the set list a few weeks before a big show. He kept his cool all through a tense audition, and he's the best player they've heard. They hire him and promise him a say in the set list. What is likely to follow?
choices: He stays calm, since he kept his cool all through a tense audition.
He settles in for good, now that he has a real say in the set list.
Before a big show, a fight over the set list blows up and he quits.
questions.explanation: Three fights over the set list before big shows is his pattern, and patterns repeat. One calm audition is a single moment, and a say in the songs is the very thing he fought over before.

questions.prompt: Your brother says, "I keep lending my car to my friend. He's dented it twice, but he apologized so sweetly, and he's a good guy at heart. He wants it again on Saturday." How do you answer him?
choices: Lend it again, since a kind heart counts for more than a couple of dents.
Two dents say more than two apologies, so keep the keys this time.
Give your friend one more chance, but call it the last.
questions.explanation: Denting the car twice is what your friend keeps doing, and sweet apologies don't change it. Calling the next try the last one still bets the car on the same pattern.

questions.prompt: A start-up hires an engineer for a kind of project she has never done. At every past job, she raised problems early, even when it made her look bad. Three weeks in, she warns the team about a serious flaw. Why did hiring on her record pay off in new territory?
choices: A brand-new kind of project pushes skilled people to work harder and notice more.
Start-ups are small, so a flaw is easy for anyone on the team to spot early.
The way she handles bad news is part of her, so it came with her.
questions.explanation: Raising problems early showed up at every job, so it was her pattern, and patterns follow people into new work. In a small team, a flaw still needs someone willing to speak up.

reviewCards.front: A gym owner hired a trainer who wowed everyone at a trial class. Within a month he was skipping sessions, just as his last two gyms said he had. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She judged him on one great class and never weighed what two gyms had seen. The no-shows were his pattern, and it came along with him.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should count most when you decide whether to trust someone with something big?
reviewCards.back: What they have done again and again, especially when things went wrong. Charm, talent and promises show what they could do, not what they will do.

reviewCards.front: A fun, generous friend wants to sign a lease with you. She has left her last three leases early. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Go by the three broken leases, not the fun. Expect her to leave early again, and keep your name off a lease with her.

reviewCards.front: Why does someone's past behavior beat their promises as a guide to what they'll do next?
reviewCards.back: People repeat deep patterns laid down early in life, often without seeing them. A promise is what they hope to do. The record is what they do.

reviewCards.front: Before trusting a brilliant person with something that matters, the first thing to check is ...
reviewCards.back: ... what they have done in that same spot before, again and again, and how it went when things got hard.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Reading people by their track record, so a first impression doesn't decide for you.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to make plans that depend on someone else, I write down what that person did the last few times and plan around it.
When I catch myself thinking that this time they will be different, I list the last times it went the same way, and plan for it happening again.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tonight, pick one person you rely on for something that matters. Write down the last three times they handled it, and circle what keeps happening.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, before you agree to anything that depends on someone new, ask one person who has worked with them what they did again and again, and compare it with the pitch.

chapters.title: Why the Always-There Friend Gets Forgotten
chapters.hook: Answer every text in a minute, and people stop asking about your day. Miss one weekend, and your phone fills with messages asking where you are.
chapters.counterintuition: The usual advice is to be there for people every time they ask. Stepping back a little works better, because people value what they might lose and stop seeing what is always within reach.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When someone starts taking you for granted, pull back a little so they notice the gap and come looking.
chapters.tryThisNow: Let one message from someone who expects your instant reply wait two hours before you answer it today.

memorableLines.text: What is always there goes unseen; a small gap makes people look again.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why will people queue at dawn for a nearly sold-out sneaker, yet forget to thank the sister who drives them everywhere? The sneaker does nothing for them. The sister gives up her Saturdays. Robert Greene's answer is that people want what they cannot quite have, and stop seeing what comes too easily.

Coco Chanel, a poor girl raised in an orphanage, had nothing to offer but herself. She saw that being easy to get made people lose interest. So she never made herself fully available and kept herself a mystery. Her clothes and perfume were never pushed on everyone. She made them feel rare and hard to get. People wanted them more, and she built a fashion empire.

Greene's advice is blunt. Don't make yourself too available, make what you offer seem scarce, and step away at the right moment so others come looking. Letting a message wait or turning down a favor opens a gap, and the gap makes people imagine what they would miss. Always saying yes seems the way to be valued, but it makes you part of the furniture. When someone starts treating your help as a given, make yourself a little less available, and they'll feel the gap and come looking.

He calls it the Law of Covetousness. To covet means to want something badly, often something that belongs to someone else or sits just out of reach. People want what they cannot quite have, and they lose interest in what comes too easily. None of this is chosen. It runs below the surface, which is why the sister's family would be surprised to hear they take her for granted.

Greene's reason lies in how the mind treats what it cannot see. What is always there fades into the background. When something goes missing, the mind rushes to fill the gap. The picture it paints is often richer than the real thing ever was. People are also pulled toward whatever feels forbidden or out of reach.

Coco Chanel learned this early. She grew up poor and was raised in an orphanage, with nothing to offer the world but herself. She saw that people soon lost interest in whatever was easy to get. So she never made herself fully available. She kept herself a mystery and left people wondering about her.

She ran her work the same way. Her designs and her perfume were never pushed on everyone. She made them feel rare and hard to get, and people wanted them more for it. A poor orphan built a fashion empire, not by chasing buyers but by shaping what they wanted.

Greene's advice follows, and it is blunt. Don't make yourself too available. Hold something back, and keep a little mystery. Make what you offer feel scarce, and use the pull of what seems out of reach. Above all, step away at the right moment, so the other person feels the gap and comes looking. In ordinary life, that can mean letting a message wait, skipping one visit or turning down a favor.

The same hunger works on you. You may chase the friend who rarely calls and barely notice the one who always does. It is the same pull that makes people overlook whoever is always on hand.

So think back to the sister in the car. Always saying yes seems the surest way to be valued, yet it does the opposite. What never goes missing stops being seen, and she has become part of the furniture. One Saturday when she is busy will make her family notice her more than a year of rides. When someone starts treating your help as a given, make yourself a little less available, and they'll feel the gap and come looking.

examples.title: Edits that land at 10:40 at night
examples.scenario: Joaquín edits videos from his spare room for a travel company that pays half his rent. For a year he has answered their messages within minutes, even on weekends. Now the owner sends "tiny changes" at 10:40 at night and hasn't said thanks in months. Tonight a new one pings in while Joaquín is eating dinner. His thumb hovers over the reply button.
examples.whatToDo: Finish dinner, leave the message until nine the next morning, and from now on answer this client during working hours.
examples.whyItMatters: When the instant replies stop, the owner notices how much Joaquín's speed was worth and starts treating his time with care.

examples.title: When the study group stops saying thanks
examples.scenario: Sunita takes an online bookkeeping course after her day job. Every Sunday she posts her neat summary notes in the study group chat, and lately classmates ask for them before watching the lectures. Hoping for some thanks, she made the notes color-coded and longer. It cost her three late nights. The only reply in the chat was a thumbs-up and "ok, send next week's."
examples.whatToDo: Skip posting the notes this Sunday, stay friendly in the chat, and share them only with whoever asks for them directly.
examples.whyItMatters: A Sunday without the notes lets the group feel the gap, and her work turns from something expected into something sought.

examples.title: A damp towel on the folded pile
examples.scenario: For years Yetunde has washed and folded the laundry for everyone in her house. Tonight her grown son drops a damp towel on the clean pile and says, "Mum, I need my blue shirt for the morning." Heat rises in her face. Part of her wants to shout at him. Part of her wants to stop touching his clothes for good.
examples.whatToDo: Skip both the shouting and the strike. Say calmly that his washing is his this week, and leave his basket by the machine.
examples.whyItMatters: A week of hunting for his own clean shirt lets him feel the gap, while the warmth between them stays whole.

questions.prompt: For a year, Tomás drove his brother to the airport whenever asked, and the brother stopped saying thanks. Last month Tomás said he was busy twice. Now his brother calls ahead and thanks him. Why did the change work?
choices: His brother felt guilty about the past year and wanted to make amends.
Once the rides were no longer certain, his brother saw what they were worth.
His brother began to worry that someone else now came first, and he grew jealous.
questions.explanation: Two missed rides made his brother feel what the rides had been worth all year. Nothing in Tomás's busy weeks points to a rival, so jealousy does not explain the new thanks.

questions.prompt: You have hosted the monthly book club in your living room for two years. Lately members arrive late, skip the reading and leave their cups for you to wash. What should you do?
choices: Write a short list of house rules and send it to everyone before the next meeting.
Bake something special and pick an exciting book to win back their interest.
Say you're taking next month off hosting and let someone else have a turn.
questions.explanation: A month without your living room lets the group feel what you have been giving them. House rules push harder on people who have stopped noticing your effort, but they don't make anyone miss it.

questions.prompt: Ama stays after every choir rehearsal to stack the chairs, hoping the others will see how much she gives. A year on, they walk past her without a word. What went wrong in her thinking?
choices: She believed that always being on hand would make the others value her more.
She believed the others were simply too tired after rehearsal to notice what she did.
She believed stacking chairs was the only way to earn a place there.
questions.explanation: Staying after every rehearsal turned her help into something nobody saw anymore, because it was always there. Tiredness after one rehearsal would not explain a whole year of silence.

questions.prompt: Lin's neighbor has watered his plants every time he travels, and Lin now just leaves the key with a short note. This time, the neighbor says she is away that weekend too. What is most likely to happen next?
choices: Lin feels hurt, and he stops asking the neighbor for any help.
Lin sees what the help was worth and asks more warmly next time.
Lin finds another neighbor to water the plants and soon forgets the first one.
questions.explanation: Missing the help once lets Lin feel what it was worth, so his next request comes with real thanks. One busy weekend is too small a gap to send him elsewhere for good.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My sister treats me like a free babysitter. I'm going to stop answering her calls for a whole month." What is the best reply?
choices: "Say no to the next babysitting request, but keep picking up her calls."
"Good idea, a month of silence will show her what she's missing."
"Ask her to do something for you in return, so the favors feel even."
questions.explanation: Turning down one babysitting night lets the sister feel the gap while the two stay close. A month of ignored calls goes well past a small, friendly step back.

questions.prompt: For years a teacher ran a free Saturday yoga class in the park, and fewer people came each month. Then she skipped three Saturdays. When she returned, the lawn was full, and people said they'd missed it. Why did the break bring them back?
choices: The break gave people time to tell their friends about the class.
The teacher came back rested after the break, so her classes felt fresher and better.
Without the class, people felt the empty Saturday and missed what it gave them.
questions.explanation: Week after week, the class had faded into the background. Three empty Saturdays made people feel what it gave them, and they said so. A rested teacher does not explain why they missed it.

questions.prompt: For a year you've driven three friends to the climbing gym every Saturday. Lately they just text "leaving in 5?" and never offer gas money. What is your move this week?
choices: Tell them you'll skip driving this Saturday and meet them at the gym.
Stop driving for good and let them figure out their own rides from now on.
Ask each friend to chip in for gas, starting this coming Saturday.
questions.explanation: Skipping one Saturday lets your friends feel what the rides were worth while you still climb together. Gas money would cover the cost but leave them just as used to you.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what's the move when someone starts treating your help as a given?
reviewCards.back: Pull back a little: say no once, or be slower to answer, so they feel the gap and come looking for you.

reviewCards.front: A coworker now drops every stuck file on your desk without asking, as if you were the help desk.
reviewCards.back: Say you're busy the next time, just once, and stay friendly. A day without your help shows them what it was worth, and they start asking first.

reviewCards.front: Why does someone who is sometimes out of reach get valued more than someone always on hand?
reviewCards.back: People stop seeing what comes easily. When something goes missing, they feel the gap and imagine what they would lose.

reviewCards.front: When you step back from someone who takes you for granted, keep the step small, because ...
reviewCards.back: ... the aim is to be missed, not gone. You stay friendly and are simply less on hand.

reviewCards.front: Every Monday a man brought homemade lunch for his whole office, hoping it would make them value him. Now coworkers grumble when he forgets.
reviewCards.back: He thought always giving would earn their thanks, but steady giving became expected. Skipping a Monday now and then would have let them miss it.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Noticing when your help has become expected, and making yourself a bit scarcer so it is valued again.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I first check my messages in the morning, I pick one request from someone who always counts on me, and answer it after lunch.
When I catch myself about to say yes to someone who never says thanks, I say I can't this time, kindly, with no long excuse.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, turn down one small favor from someone who has stopped thanking you, and stay friendly while you say it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, pick one person who leans on you without noticing. Skip one thing you always do for them, stay warm, and see whether they come looking.

chapters.title: Judge Big Choices by Where They Leave You Next Year
chapters.hook: You're about to grab the offer that ends at midnight, and it feels smart. How it feels tonight says nothing about next year.
chapters.counterintuition: We tend to trust a choice that looks good right now and leave later for later. What works is picturing where it leaves you a year from now, since the rush of the moment hides the chain of effects that follows.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before a big choice, picture where it leaves you in a year, and judge it by that.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one real choice in front of you today, picture where each option leaves you a year from now, and choose by that.

memorableLines.text: A choice is only as good as the place it leaves you next year.

breakdown.fastRead:
The choice that feels best today is often the one you regret a year from now. Robert Greene shows it with the South Sea Company. John Blunt, who helped run it, dreamed up a plan to turn the country's debt into company shares, and people rushed to buy. Isaac Newton, the famous scientist, bought early and sold at a profit. As the price kept climbing, he bought back in near the top. When it crashed, he lost a fortune.

If a genius can fall for this, so can you. Greene calls it shortsightedness: people get swept up in what is happening now and lose sight of where it leads. A climbing price shouts, while next year stays quiet. His fix is to step back and judge today by what it will bring months and years ahead. He wants that long view to become a habit, not just a check before big choices.

Say a store offers you a sofa with nothing to pay for a year. Notice how much you want it. Then picture yourself a year on: the payments have started, eating your trip fund. From there, you choose the cheaper sofa you can afford now. Measure each big choice by the life it hands you a year from now, and today's rush loses its grip.

Greene names signs that this force has a hold on you, and each one keeps your eyes on today. One is unintended consequences. examples.title: A camper van with a noon deadline
examples.scenario: Elif's partner, Joon, sends her a link at eleven at night: a used camper van, far cheaper than any they've seen. The seller wants an answer by noon. They've talked about road trips for years. The van would also eat most of the money they've saved for a home of their own. Elif sits up in bed, thumb over the reply.
examples.whatToDo: Picture the two of you a year from now, with the van parked outside and the home fund nearly empty. Decide together from there.
examples.whyItMatters: A noon deadline makes the van feel urgent. A year out, she can see which dream it costs them.

examples.title: Night shifts picked from a list
examples.scenario: Before switching to nights at the parcel depot, Tariq wrote a pros-and-cons list on the back of a delivery slip. Every line was about the next few weeks: more pay per hour, a quiet loading dock, no boss watching. Ten months on, the money is real. But he dropped the day course that would have made him a shift supervisor, and the job went to someone else.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the list, but add one line at the top: where each shift leaves him a year from now. Weigh that line first.
examples.whyItMatters: His list judged nights by the first few weeks. A year out would have shown the supervisor job slipping away.

examples.title: When a friend says the lab can wait
examples.scenario: Aoife has a place in a summer research program that will count toward her final-year project. Her friend Lucía wants her at a beach kayak-rental stand instead, with good money and long sunny afternoons. When Aoife hesitates over the sign-up sheet, Lucía laughs. "You're twenty. The lab will still be there next year." Aoife feels like the dull one.
examples.whatToDo: Walk Lucía through the start of final year: the kayak money spent, or the project underway. Choose by that picture.
examples.whyItMatters: Lucía is arguing for this summer. Next year's picture gives Aoife an answer that isn't about being dull.

questions.prompt: A friend asks you to put your savings into her food truck. All month the line has wrapped around the block, and she has already shown you this month's sales, her best ever. What do you do?
choices: Say yes this week, since a line that long proves the truck is working.
Ask to see last week's sales too before making up your mind.
Imagine your savings and the truck a year on, and decide by that.
questions.explanation: A long line shows this month, not where your savings stand next year. Imagining both a year on judges the deal by where it leaves you. More sales figures from these same weeks have the same blind spot.

questions.prompt: A dental hygienist quits her steady job to sell sneakers online. Her sales have doubled every week this month. What trap has she fallen into?
choices: Letting one hot month decide a move that shapes her next year.
Quitting without first sitting down to write out all the pros and cons.
Selling only sneakers when a wider range of goods is safer.
questions.explanation: A month of doubling sales is this month's news, and quitting shapes her whole next year. A pros-and-cons list built on that same hot month would still point her the same way.

questions.prompt: The bank will lend a couple enough for a big house across town. Before signing, they picture the year ahead: the payments, the long drive and a baby due in spring. What most likely happens next?
choices: They sign anyway, since the bank has said yes and the house feels right.
They see the payments and drive squeezing the baby's first year, and rethink.
They get lost in what-ifs and let the house slip away.
questions.explanation: Picturing the year ahead puts the payments, the drive and the baby side by side, so they judge the house by that year. It points them at one year, not at endless what-ifs.

questions.prompt: A coworker says, "This coin rose all week. I'm moving my holiday savings into it today, and I'll work out when to sell later." What do you say back?
choices: "Put in a bit more while it's rising, and the gain will be bigger."
"Check the price every day, so you can sell at the top."
"Before you buy, picture where your savings stand next year if it falls."
questions.explanation: A week of rising prices is today's news. Picturing the savings next year, in case the coin drops, judges the move by where it leaves your coworker. Watching the price daily keeps them stuck in today.

questions.prompt: A pharmacist is offered a manager job with more pay and a two-hour drive each way. After a week of thinking it over, she still wants it. Then she pictures a year in, sees her pottery class and her sleep gone, and says no. Why did picturing the year help her?
choices: It slowed her down so the first rush could fade before she answered.
The picture of next year showed costs the shiny offer hid today.
It made the extra pay look smaller than it really was.
questions.explanation: Today the offer looked like pure gain. A year in, the long drive had eaten her class and her sleep, so she could judge the job by where it left her. A week of waiting had not shown her that.

questions.prompt: At a car lot, the salesperson says the deal on monthly payments ends at closing. You love the car. What is your move?
choices: Ask where these payments leave you a year on, then decide from there.
Push hard for a bigger discount, since the salesperson clearly wants the sale today.
Look up owner reviews of the car on your phone first.
questions.explanation: A deal that ends at closing makes tonight feel like the only moment that counts. Asking where the payments leave you a year on judges the car by next year. Reviews tell you about the car, not your budget.

questions.prompt: A student takes every extra shift at a ski rental shop this winter. The pay is good, and her exams are still months off. What's the trap in her thinking?
choices: Taking the shifts by feel instead of writing down the pros and cons.
Believing exams that are months away can wait until they actually arrive.
Saying yes to each shift instead of sleeping on it first.
questions.explanation: Months off feels like later, so this winter's pay wins. Picturing her grades a year from now shows where the shifts leave her. A list of pros and cons written today would still weigh this winter's money most.

reviewCards.front: A recruiter calls with a job at a buzzy new company. The pay is higher, and they want an answer by Friday.
reviewCards.back: Picture where that job leaves you a year from now, next to where your current path leads, and decide by that, not by Friday's buzz.

reviewCards.front: Why can a choice that feels great today turn out badly a year later?
reviewCards.back: What is happening now feels loud and close, while next year feels quiet and far off. Unless you picture where the choice leads, the moment decides for you.

reviewCards.front: When a price keeps climbing and everyone around you seems to be getting rich, the question to ask before you buy is ...
reviewCards.back: ... where this money will leave me a year from now if the climb stops, because that matters more than this week's rise.

reviewCards.front: A couple adopted a big, lively dog on the spot at a weekend fair. A year later, their small flat and long work days had made life hard for all of them.
reviewCards.back: They judged the choice by the joy of that afternoon. Picturing their home and their work days a year on would have shown the strain before they signed.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what do you do before a big choice, and why?
reviewCards.back: Picture where it leaves you a year from now and decide by that, because how it feels today hides where it leads.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Looking past a choice's first thrill to see where it lands you down the road.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking I can sort a decision out later, I picture where that decision leaves me a year from now before I go on.
When I sit down to sign up for something with monthly payments, I add up a year of payments and picture where that leaves me before I sign.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before today ends, pick one choice you are weighing right now. Describe each option a year from now in one sentence, and notice which one still looks good.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, look back at one choice you made in the last seven days. Ask where it is heading a year from now, and change your next step if it points somewhere you do not want to go.

chapters.title: Why Good Arguments Make People Dig In
chapters.hook: Make a flawless case, and the person across the table folds their arms. Your best reasons are what made them dig in.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think strong facts will win anyone over. Actually, people come round when they feel smart, free and good, because a push feels like an attack on how they see themselves.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you want someone on your side, make them feel smart, free and good before you ask for anything.
chapters.tryThisNow: Ask one person today for their advice on something they know well, and listen to the whole answer.

memorableLines.text: Win their pride first, and the yes often follows.

breakdown.fastRead:
Mateus works at Hilde's hardware store, where she orders stock in a paper ledger. He has printed a spreadsheet proving the ledger costs them sales, and he is sure it will win her over. He plans to lay it on her counter. But the sheet tells Hilde she has run her shop badly for years. She will dig in, and the empty shelves will stay.

Robert Greene calls this the Law of Defensiveness. Everyone holds a self-opinion, a flattering picture of themselves as free, smart and good. Push hard, even with good facts, and you seem to attack that picture, so people guard it. When Lyndon Johnson arrived in the Senate as a junior member, he did not push his ideas. He listened to the powerful senators, asked their advice and built them up, above all Richard Russell. Russell backed the young man who made him feel admired, and Johnson rose to majority leader, the senator who leads the bigger party.

Mateus leaves the printout in his bag. He asks Hilde how she knows what to reorder, and says nobody knows the customers better. Then he asks if she'd track paint stock on the laptop, her choice. She says she might. Once you make people feel smart, free and good before you ask, their guard drops and they come your way.
