The years pass faster than they feel, and every day spent drifting is one you do not get back.

Feeling the end this way does not weigh you down. It gives you urgency and focus. Once you know your days are limited, you stop handing them to whatever happens to be in front of you, and you start asking what deserves them. Next to that question, petty fears and grudges shrink.

examples.title: An old friend passing through tonight
examples.scenario: Thabo's oldest friend, Dumi, texts that he's driving through town tonight and could stop by for an hour. Thabo has just come home from a long shift. His shoes are off and a new episode is waiting on the screen. The two of them have said "next time" for three years now. His thumb hovers over the reply, "Rain check, mate?"
examples.whatToDo: Remember that next times run out, delete the rain check, and tell Dumi to come round for the hour.
examples.whyItMatters: Three years of next times is how old friendships quietly fade, and the episode will still be there on Sunday.

examples.title: The specials board that stayed blank
examples.scenario: Mirela manages the dining room at a busy ramen restaurant and has wanted to cook her own dishes for years. Each time the urge came, she told herself she would start once things calmed down. They never did. Last month the old head cook, who had offered to teach her his broth, retired and moved away. She feels it most at three o'clock, when the room sits empty.
examples.whatToDo: Tell herself plainly that her years are counted, and use today's empty three o'clock hour to cook one dish for the specials board.
examples.whyItMatters: Waiting for things to calm down already cost her a teacher, and the next chance would slip away just as quietly.

examples.title: A long weekend before the anatomy exam
examples.scenario: Ximena is a second-year nursing student. Her grandmother, who taught her to make tamales, lives a six-hour bus ride away, and Ximena wants to spend the long weekend there. Her study partner rolls her eyes. "Don't be so gloomy, she'll be around for years. Stay and cram anatomy with me." Ximena feels silly and starts unpacking her bag.
examples.whatToDo: Zip the bag back up, tell her partner kindly that nobody's years are promised, and study the anatomy notes on the bus.
examples.whyItMatters: Exams come round every term, but weekends with her grandmother are limited, and a friend's comfort shouldn't spend them for her.

questions.prompt: After a friend's funeral, a man in his fifties starts each Sunday by telling himself plainly that his years are limited. Then he picks one thing he'd hate to leave undone that week. What will most likely happen to his weeks?
choices: He grows gloomy, and the dark mood seeps into his whole week.
He rushes into every plan at once, then drops most of them within a month.
He drifts less and finally gives time to what he kept putting off.
questions.explanation: Feeling his years are limited gives him a reason to stop drifting, so the things he put off finally get time. He picks one thing a week, not everything at once, so a rush and crash is unlikely.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'll visit my brother in Chile once work calms down. There's always next year." What's the most useful thing to say back?
choices: "None of us is promised next year. Could you go this year instead?"
"Put the trip in your calendar now for next year, so it really happens."
"Smart, a calmer year will make the trip far more relaxing."
questions.explanation: Saying next year isn't promised turns someday into a choice your friend can make now. Writing the trip down for next year keeps it parked in someday, where things wait while time runs out.

questions.prompt: A hospice worker says sitting with dying patients has changed her days off. She no longer lets them slip away to errands and screens. Why does her work have this effect?
choices: Seeing death up close makes her own short time feel real, not just known.
Her job is so draining that she guards her days off to recover.
Caring for others all week has trained her to plan her own time more carefully.
questions.explanation: Watching patients die makes her own end feel real, not just a fact she knows, and that stops her days off from drifting. Planning skills would tidy her schedule but wouldn't change what she spends it on.

questions.prompt: It's Saturday morning, the flat is messy, and nothing is planned. For years you've meant to record your grandfather's stories about his youth. What do you do first?
choices: Tidy the messy flat first, so the stories can get your full attention later.
Tell yourself plainly your Saturdays are counted, and call your grandfather this morning.
Wait for a weekend when you feel ready for a long talk.
questions.explanation: Telling yourself plainly that Saturdays run out keeps the morning from drifting, so the call happens today. Tidying first sounds sensible, but chores easily fill the morning and push the call back to someday.

questions.prompt: A man in his thirties, busy at work all week, says he'd rather not think about death and just enjoy life. His weekends go to shopping trips and streaming, while the novel he's always wanted to write waits. Where is the trap?
choices: Thinking his job leaves him too tired to write on his weekends.
Thinking that keeping death out of mind is what lets him enjoy life.
Thinking a whole novel is too big a goal to start on short weekends.
questions.explanation: Pushing death out of mind doesn't make his weekends richer. It lets them drift while the novel waits for someday. Being tired might slow him, but the deeper trouble is acting as if time won't run out.

questions.prompt: After a scary night in the emergency room, a woman spends a week doing everything she'd put off. Then she decides to stop dwelling on it and puts the thought away. What most likely happens next?
choices: The old drift creeps back once the thought of her limited time fades.
That one week of urgency resets her habits for the rest of the year.
She feels lighter and has more energy for the things she loves.
questions.explanation: Her week of action came from feeling her time was short. Once she puts that thought away, nothing pulls her back toward what counts. One burst can't hold her habits without the reminder coming back.

questions.prompt: Over lunch you mention that remembering your time is limited helps you plan your weekends. A coworker laughs. "That's so morbid. You're thirty, relax." What's a good answer?
choices: "Maybe, but you should try it too, before it's too late."
"Fair point, I only do it on bad weeks when I need perspective."
"It doesn't feel gloomy to me. It stops my weekends drifting by."
questions.explanation: Saying plainly what the reminder does for you answers the worry and keeps the habit. Saving it for bad weeks gives the reminder up most of the time, and the weekends drift again.

reviewCards.front: When you catch yourself saying you'll start the thing that matters once life calms down, the first move is ...
reviewCards.back: ... to tell yourself plainly that your time is limited, then give that thing a piece of today, not someday.

reviewCards.front: A man kept every thought of death out of his head to stay cheerful. Ten years on, the language course he meant to take is still unopened. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: Keeping death out of mind didn't make his life fuller. It let him act as if time would never run out, so the course waited for a someday that never came.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should you do with the fact that your time is short?
reviewCards.back: Bring it to mind often, and let it push today's hours toward the things that matter most to you.

reviewCards.front: Sunday afternoon, nothing planned. For months you've meant to visit the aunt who raised you. The remote is already in your hand.
reviewCards.back: Tell yourself plainly that these Sundays are counted, put the remote down, and call her now to say you're coming over.

reviewCards.front: Why does remembering that you will die make people waste less time instead of just feeling worse?
reviewCards.back: A limit you can feel brings urgency. You stop drifting and putting things off, and you start choosing what deserves your days.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Turning the fact that your days run out into a reason to choose how you spend this one.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking I'll get to something important someday, I tell myself plainly that my days are counted, and give that thing twenty minutes today.
When I sit down on the sofa after work with a free evening, I ask what I would hate to have left undone, and give it the first hour.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before you go to bed tonight, spend one full hour on the thing you would most hate to have left undone. Do it before any screen comes on.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the start of each week, tell yourself plainly that this is one of a limited number of weeks. Name the one thing it should hold, and protect an hour for it before Wednesday.
